## Instructions

Write complete arguments, not only calculations. You may discuss broad ideas with classmates, but write your own solutions and list collaborators. Cite any permitted source beyond the text and course notes.

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">1</span> **Definitions in action.** Let $a,b,c\in\mathbb Z$. Prove directly from the definition of divisibility that if $a\mid b$ and $b\mid c$, then $a\mid c$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">2</span> **Remainder classes.** Prove that the square of every integer is congruent to $0$, $1$, or $4$ modulo $8$. Is each of the three possibilities attained?
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">3</span> **A divisibility test.** Prove that an integer is divisible by $3$ if and only if the sum of its decimal digits is divisible by $3$.

<details class="hint"><summary>Hint</summary>
Use $10\equiv1\pmod3$ and write the integer in decimal expansion.
</details>
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">4</span> **Euclidean algorithm.** Compute $\gcd(2026,748)$ and express the gcd as $2026x+748y$ for integers $x,y$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">5</span> **Linear equations.** Determine whether $84x+126y=30$ has an integer solution. If it does, find all integer solutions; if it does not, prove impossibility.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">6</span> **Modular inverse.** Find the least nonnegative inverse of $37$ modulo $101$, and verify the answer by multiplication.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">7</span> **A structural gcd identity.** Prove that for every positive integer $n$,

$$\gcd(n,n+1)=1.$$

Then generalize: determine $\gcd(n,n+k)$ in terms of $n$ and $k$.
</div>

<div class="problem">
<span class="problem-number">8</span> **Exploration before proof.** Compute $\gcd(F_m,F_n)$ for several Fibonacci numbers and formulate a conjecture. Prove one nontrivial special case of your conjecture, clearly indicating which Fibonacci identities you use.
</div>

## Optional challenge

Prove that consecutive Fibonacci numbers are relatively prime using the Euclidean algorithm rather than a closed formula.
